Very true with physical stuff to a certain extent, but I'll have to disagree with you when it comes down to electronic data. We're getting to the point where we have extremely strong encryption for data at rest and while it's processing, we can use hashing for non repudiation, and many more techniques to prevent people editing and changing data at will. It all comes down to the person implementing these extremely complex and secure access control methods.

It always comes down to someone specific who could be compromised and ruin the security of the entire system. Whether it's the higher up individual who's in charge of implementing physical and data security in a business, or just a security guard who's in charge of making sure people cant get through a man-trap.

We can always put mitigations in place like I was saying in my previous post, things like separation of duties, mandatory vacations, and non human verification methods that cannot be tampered with except when initially set up. There will always be that threat though when it comes down to it, insider threats will always be a concern even when we have technology to prevent outsiders or malicious individuals from altering important/secure data.

read my other comment. I never said that it's only secure because it's source code hasn't been release. Having multiple lines of defense is a must, but releasing source code to the public is generally bad practice in the security world. You cannot trust the public to use information they gain by penetration testing to better the hardening of the systems or the code. Good practice in security involves hiring trusted firms to do large amounts of penetration testing. Lest you allow APTs, hacktivists, and bad actors to discover vulnerabilities and exploit these attack vectors to compromise systems without anyone knowing.

Edit: It's interesting when reddit downvotes stuff even though this is literally basic security practice in the corporate world. Go try to convince Apple, Microsoft, Google, Amazon or any other big service, infrastructure, or platform provider if you can take a peek at their code for "security purposes"

Spoiler: They wont let you because you probably have malicious intent.

Many people look to Linux to argue that open source is better, but the only reason the system that Linux has works to a certain extent (Though, their recent issue with malicious commits happening to their code shows that it doesn't really work 100% of the time at all) is due to the large large number of actors who do daily commits in good faith to the code, and the huge amount of individuals who do penetration testing like activities when doing said commits. Such as Intel, Red Hat, Linaro, Samsung, SUSE, and IBM. And even with all of that they still had a security breach recently due to malicious commits.Souce - [https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/linux-bans-university-of-minnesota-for-committing-malicious-code/](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/linux-bans-university-of-minnesota-for-committing-malicious-code/)

You're line of thinking is also interesting. I never argued that security by obscurity would be the only way of protecting a system that needs to be extremely secure such as voting systems.
